Mr. Speaker, while I am at it I should like to reply to a question asked on January 12 by the hon. member for Cumberland in connection with the hiring policy of Expo '67. The hiring policy of the Canadian Corporation for the World Exhibition has always aimed and continues to aim at achieving a balance between English speaking and French speaking Canadians and at ensuring the greatest possible representation of Canadians from all parts of the country, having regard to the fact that Expo '67 is a national undertaking.
At the senior level, for example, the management of C.C.W.E. comprises four English speaking Canadians and five French speaking Canadians. There are 26 branch heads in the six departments of the corporation; 10 of these are English speaking Canadians and 16 are French speaking Canadians. It should be realized, however, that it is not always possible to achieve the balance throughout at more junior levels and in all individual units of staff. The labour market in the Montreal area is predominantly French Canadian, and while the C.C.W.E. has underwritten moving expenses for employees hired throughout Canada at senior levels, it did not seem appropriate to extend such practice to the junior levels. While the C.C.W.E. has recognized the need to achieve balance, it should be borne in mind that its hiring policies are based predominantly on qualifications. The C.C.W.E. is confident that it has brought together an effective group of qualified Canadians.
In the case of the youth pavilion-which was the particular unit to which the question applied-for which program staff is currently
Inquiries of the Ministry being hired, another factor is the short period of employment which makes it even less advisable to pay for moving expenditures and tends to limit the area from which certain classes of employees can be drawn. However, the production staff of the youth pavilion are bilingual and they continue to obtain guidance from the youth advisory committee made up of representatives of 32 organizations from all parts of the country. The youth program itself is to be fully bilingual and broadly international.
A few positions remain to be filled on the youth pavilion staff, and the C.C.W.E. will cont nue to aim at the best possible balance, all factors considered. If there are English speaking Canadians who feel themselves qualified and who wish to apply, they are invited by the C.C.W.E. to do so.

Yesterday afternoon while I was in Montreal I met with the regional officer of the bankruptcy branch and Mr. Peter Lawrence of the firm of chartered accountants of McDonald, Currie, the trustee under the
January 19, 1967

proposals. At this stage the debtors, Messrs. S. L. and N. H. Caplan and their company, Depositors Mortgage Corporation, have made two proposals to their creditors under section 27 of the Brankruptcy Act. Both proposals contemplate a payment to the creditors of one hundred cents on the dollar over a period of years. The preliminary statement of assests and liabilities indicates that there is a surplus of assets over liabilities in the case of Depositors Mortgage Corporation in the amount of $647,000-odd, and in the case of the two Caplans personally in the amount of $343,000-odd.
The superintendent of bankruptcy, who reports to the Registrar General, has a duty which is a supervisory one over the administration of any bankruptcy or proposal. The trustee undertook to report to the superintendent of bankruptcy through the regional officer in Montreal all relevant information regarding the nature of the business carried on by the debtors or relating to the causes of any insolvency. He has also undertaken to advise the superintendent whether in his opinion there were any irregularities within the meaning of the Brankruptcy Act leading up to the proposal. The trustee gave it to me as his preliminary opinion that on the basis of the facts as he now knows them, there does not appear to have been any irregularity on the part of the debtors. The primary cause of the current situation would appear to be one of liquidity caused by the pressure of short term money invested on long term against the security of real estate.

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
maintopic: COLUMBIA RIVER-PROPOSED FURTHER DEVELOPMENT BY U.S.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, a rapid examination of this question by my officials leads me to make the following points, which you may allow me to put on record.
1.	Additional installation at Grand Coulee will be installed to meet very short term peak loads on the United States system.
2.	The limited amount of stored water required for such peaking operation will be, and in fact must be, provided from the reservoir of Grand Coulee itself. It is not practical to try to operate distant Canadian storages to provide this service and there is no treaty requirement for such operation. Canadian storages will be operated to provide a seasonal regulating service, not a daily or weekly peaking service.

I had better raise my voice, Mr. Chairman. For several days the committee has been discussing what was referred to as the Magna Carta of the west, the Crowsnest pass rates, and I find it difficult to reconcile some of the minister's statements on that subject with the lack of any protection in this new section against action which the commission might take with respect to the Maritime Freight Rates Act which, so far as transportation is concerned, is the Magna Carta of the
January 19, 1967

east. It is rather an anomaly that the new transportation policy, which we all agree is proper and should be proceeded with, is being considered without regard to the interests of four of the ten provinces.
Undoubtedly the minister is aware from some reports he has received to date on the Atlantic transportation study that the Maritime Freight Rates Act will have to be examined very critically, and perhaps amended in terms of a more modern Canada; because even with the assistance of that act the position of the east has been eroded and is still being eroded. I go back to that act as the Magna Carta of the east and state that something should be said in legislative form about protection for the east under it. No doubt the minister is sincere in his expressed intent, but that intent is not the law of the land, and his expressions in that regard will not be read with too much interest two or three years from now when this bill is being enforced.
In 1927 the Duncan commission said the position of the east relative to the rest of the country had deteriorated from the time of the Intercolonial Railway. It stated that from 1876 to 1912 the position of the east had been easy and relatively constant with the rest of Canada, but since 1912 it had deteriorated. This was the reason for the introduction of the Maritime Freight Rates Act. We are now considering a brand new bill which is supposed to resolve all of Canada's transportation problems but there is no specific mention in it, particularly in new section 335, of protection for the rates structures in the east. I would like to know whether the minister has reconsidered the suggested amendment which I read into the record last night with respect to maintaining the rates freeze until the transportation commission's study has been completed and until the government moves to implement new legislation for the east.
Considering the way governments work I firmly believe that at the end of the two years freeze the government will be inclined to let the Maritime Freight Rates Act stand as it is. I believe there will not be the necessary catalyst and stimulus to bring it up to date.
I admit that the suggested amendment which I read into the record may not have been drafted in the best possible form, and lest there be any misunderstanding I wish to state I have no intention of doing away with the Maritime Freight Rates Act. But in view of the spirit of compromise which has existed and the constructive way in which consideration of this legislation has
Transportation
been proceeding, especially yesterday, I wonder if the minister would consider another suggestion with reference to new section 335 (3) I suggest that in new subsection 3 all the words after the word "thereof" be deleted and the following substituted for them:
-and thereafter shall be governed by the intent and purpose of the Maritime Freight Rates Act.
It would then read as follows:
(3) Subsections (1) and (2) shall be in force during the two years after the coming into force thereof and thereafter shall be governed by the intent and purpose of the Maritime Freight Rates Act.
The minister has intimated that at some stage, presumably after the maritime transportation study, the Maritime Freight Rates Act will have to be re-examined. I point out that the intent and purpose of that act remain the same today as they did following the Duncan commission report, namely to maintain the east in a relative position with the other parts of Canada. I wonder whether the minister will give consideration to my suggested amendment so that whatever rates are set at the end of two years will be set in accordance with the intent and purpose of the Maritime Freight Rates Act. If that cannot be considered, then I will have to decide whether or not I intend to move a formal amendment.
[DOT] (3:30 p.m.)
At the moment I am disposed to move a formal amendment in respect of the suggestion I put forward last night to the effect that the freeze be continued inasmuch as the government will be stimulated by the two railways to take action. Otherwise this would be left up to the initiative of the government and sometimes even when the government has had the best motives and principles it has been rather inert in this regard. There is no question in my mind concerning who will bring the greatest pressure to bear on the minister two or three years hence. I am sure the presidents of both railways will attempt to get the government to act. It has taken years to get this far. I do not think we should assume that after the freeze is over the government will on its own initiative take a critical look at the situation in the east. I think the danger is that it will drift along.
If the freeze continues for two years, I believe that after the two years the two railway presidents, who already have indicated that they do not like the freeze even for the two years, will be the catalyst which will cause the Minister of Transport to take some action.

I should like to know whether the minister has reconsidered his position in respect of what he said last night. I would hope that there might be a spirit of compromise so that the east would get something.

It has become obvious to those in the maritimes that the whole national transportation picture is somewhat invidious unless something is done. The west has fought and won a good fight. It is now high time that something be written into this bill to give some protection to the east.
What the minister has in his hand now is a compromise, I think, of both positions. It is not a suggestion that the freeze continue indefinitely or in perpetuity but rather that whatever rates are set after the two years be set having in mind the intent and purpose of the Maritime Freight Rates Act. I say this with the knowledge that the Maritime Freight Rates Act is a special act and can be changed in the future. The minister has indicated that it may be changed. However, whatever the changes are they should be made in such a way that they retain the intent and purpose which parliament had in mind when the legislation was first introduced. That intent and purpose are to ensure that the position of the east is relative to the position of the rest of Canada. The act even in its present form, although it is not doing the best job, at least is better than nothing. Perhaps I could interject at this point. I have worded my suggested amendment in this way because of what the minister said last night. I appreciate that the Maritime Freight Rates Act and the Crowsnest pass rates agreement are separate from this transport bill. As the minister has stated, there is no doubt that the Maritime Freight Rates Act will be considered and likely changed at some time.
When the transportation study has been made I am sure this act could be revised radically, depending on the recommendations emanating from that study. I admit I had difficulty in framing my amendment but my intent was to have the principle involved remain in existence for perhaps 20 years rather than two, or at least until the government does something about it.
I am sorry that we do not seem to have the same spirit of compromise which existed yesterday. In any event, whether the principle of the Maritime Freight Rates Act is revised or amended or thrown out completely in two or three years time, or whenever the government proposes, that principle should be the governing factor in the establishment of any rate structure. There is nothing in the bill now before us which guarantees the continuation of that principle in spite of the fact the bill is supposed to settle all the transportation problems we have encountered since confederation.
I think this measure represents a sincere attempt on the part of the minister to group certain things together. We all know there are many problems in the transportation field, and it will be five or ten years after the adoption of this measure before we can appreciate its full implications. Many things will have to be defined. Keeping that fact in mind we must take steps to make sure that the principle of the Maritime Freight Rates Act is continued. I believe it will be some time before the principle to which I have referred is changed, but whatever changes take place

as a result of the adoption of this new transportation measure, which is supposed to be a transportation Magna Carta, we wish to ensure that at least the intent and purpose of the Maritime Freight Rates Act and the Crows-nest pass agreement are maintained.
One of the things which helped to advance the idea of confederation was the promise that there would be an intercolonial railway, and we need one in order to travel and transport our goods. It is even difficult today to travel and sh.p goods at the present rate structure, but the minister knows as well as I that the provisions of the Maritime Freight Rates Act helped to solve a great number of our problems. It can continue to do so today as it did when it was first adopted.
If there is no agreement to the suggestion I have made I am inclined to move the amendment which I suggested last night to continue this principle indefinitely. The premiers of the maritime provinces have made it clear that they cannot support a transportation policy without economic considerations written into it which take into account the size and geographic location of these provinces. We wish to go along with the suggestion regarding a national transportation policy in the interest of Canada, but we certainly must protect our own position. We all know from what we have heard at committee hearings and in this chamber that transportation costs represent the biggest cost of production in the east. No matter what course the government may follow in the future in respect of maintaining, changing or amending the Maritime Freight Rates Act, the original intent and purpose, to provide reasonable equity in transportation costs in the east and in the west, must be maintained, and that is in effect what we are suggesting here.

Mr. Chairman, I hope I can show the same spirit of conciliation that hon. members have been kind enough to say I have shown hitherto. I would not claim, however, anything like the extravagant attributes given to this bill by hon. gentlemen. This bill will not solve all our transportation problems. It does not purport to do so. It purports to do two basic th'ngs. First, it will establish a single transportation agency which will deal with all forms of transportation under federal jurisdiction. I am sure that everyone agrees that generally this bill seems to improve the situation. Second, by this bill we are attempting to get away from the general structure of railway freight rates we have had in the past, under which all rates were set by

the Board of Transport Commissioners, or had to be approved by that board which established maximum and minimum rates and allowed rates to fluctuate. In exchange for this greater freedom it is proposed that the huge subsidies now being paid to the railways will be phased out. I think one would say they are the two main objectives of the bill.
[DOT] (3:50 p.m.)
I said last night, and I repeat, that I think it is unfortunate that the MacPherson commission was not able to complete its study. As the commissioners said in their report, they did not have time to consider the effects of the Maritime Freight Rates Act and its adequacy at the present time. After consultation with the governments of the Atlantic provinces the present government set up the study that is now going on and is nearing completion, not just of the Maritime Freight Rates Act-that is one element of it-but of the whole problem of transportation within the Atlantic provinces and between the Atlantic provinces and the rest of Canada. What the government in office, whatever government it may be, may do when that study has been received and analysed is something that none of us here can predict at the moment.
Therefore in framing legislation I had really no option as Minister of Transport but to accept the facts as they are at the present time and to say that at the present time I was not prepared to advance my own policies to deal with this problem, because I thought we needed much more expertise to deal with it than I have or that my department has without outside help and without time to give he matter adequate consideration. I am sure every hon. member from the Atlantic provinces would agree with that view.
We then decided to do two novel things in this bill with respect to the Atlantic provinces. The so-called At and East grain rates would have expired and the grain rates to the ports of Halifax and Saint John would have gone up. They were simply kept down by a voluntary act on the part of the railways. A year ago I was able to persuade my colleagues that we should pay a subsidy to the railways to make sure that those rates did not go up, to make sure that they stayed at the level they were then in order to have rates that would encourage the flow of grain through the Atlantic ports. I have no apology to make for doing that. I think it was a good thing to do. I think it was a good use of the taxpayers' money and I would defend it anywhere. I put it in this bill; it is in new section 329A. We

Yes. In this bill we have really departed, so far as rates are concerned, from the status quo in two respects only. One is to underwrite the At and East grain rates and the other is to continue the freeze imposed in 1959, which is being abandoned in the rest of Canada, and to add coal and certain lumber rates to that freeze for two years. The reason that provision was put in the bill was that we were not able to deal with the particular problem of the Atlantic provinces in a constructive way at this time because we did not have the necessary suggestions, the necessary elements do deal with it.
Therefore I said we were not going to worsen the position of the Atlantic provinces but were going to see that it was safeguarded for a time long enough to give the government of the day, whatever government it may be, a chance to consider that study and propose legislation to parliament. We suggested in this b.ll that the freeze should be continued for two years. We could have suggested that it be continued indefinitely instead of for two years. It seems to me it is on this point, and on this point only, that the hon. member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings and I disagree.
It is my considered judgment, since the presidents of the C.P.R. and C.N.R. do not have votes in this house and all the members from the Atlantic provinces do, that if at the end of that two-year period the government has not acted it will be much more terrified by the loss of votes in this house-I may say that I felt this keenly when the bill was drafted and I feel it even more keenly today-than they would be by the barking of the heads of the railways. I think a government faced with the prospect of having this freeze disappear, and having taken no action, would be in a terrible situation vis-avis public opinion in the Atlantic provinces.
One of my reasons for not leaving the freeze indefinite was that I thought it would be too great a temptation, if it was indefinite, for other problems that seemed more urgent in a year or two to be substituted and dealt with. There would be a tendency to say: "Oh, well, they are protected by the freeze, anyway, down there. We can forget about them
Transportation
for another year or two." On the other hand, if under the law this freeze comes to an end the government cannot forget the problem. I have had a rather long experience of the way governments behave. This experience was acquired partly as a public servant before coming into this house and has been added to by participating in government when sitting on this side of the house and observing it when sitting on the other side. Therefore I have the conviction-that is all it can be; nobody can know whether it is a fact-that a government faced with the prospect of some advantage disappearing for the Atlantic provinces would be more apt to act, and act urgently, to resolve the problem than a government that could say: Those fellows down there have the freeze; we can forget about them for two or three more years.
It is because I believe that the transportation problems of the Atlantic provinces are urgent and that the improvement of transportation in the Atlantic provinces can contribute more than anything else to the improvement of the economy of that region that I want every possible incentive to exist for government to act and deal with this problem. It is in consideration of that position that I have taken the view I have. On this one very narrow point of tactics, and not on anything else, I do not see eye to eye with the hon. member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings.
I now come to the suggested amendment of the hon. member. I would have to say that when faced with this amendment and the one he offered last night, I prefer the one he offered last night because it seems that one would have some legislative effect and I do not think this one would have any. I do not know how the transportation commission, the railways or the courts could apply the intent and purpose of the Maritime Freight Rates Act to freight rates that had been frozen for two years and were thereafter unfrozen. If, instead, the amendment said that the provisions of the Maritime Freight Rates Act should apply to these rates, that would of course make legislative sense. But it would not add one iota to the law because they apply right now and will apply during the freeze and when the freeze comes off unless parliament sees fit to change the Maritime Freight Rates Act. For that reason I would advise the hon. gentleman not to move this amendment. I do not think it would have any effect whatever except to create confusion in the mind of anyone who tried to obey the law.

With respect to the other amendment which the hon. member suggested last night, I think it is also open to very grave objection on two grounds, one of which is legislative and the other of which is political. I will deal with the legislative reason first, and perhaps I should look at the exact wording of the hon. gentleman's amendment because although he was good enough to send me a copy I seem to have mislaid it. The hon. member's amendment reads:
(3) Subsection (1) shall be in force during the two years after the coming into force of subsection (1) and shall continue in force after the said two years unless, and until, the Maritime Freight Rates Act is amended to retain the historic intent and purpose of providing Atlantic provinces industry access to the markets of Canada without the handicap of distance.
The only part of that amendment that would have any legislative effect would be the following wording "unless, and until, the Maritime Freight Rates Act is amended". As the hon. gentleman knows, that would not bind any future parliament because notwithstanding the fact that these words were there the subsection could be repealed in the next session of parliament. However, this wording would indicate a certain purpose and intent at the present time.
Nevertheless I would not be willing to support this purpose and intent because while the amendment would indicate that this parliament in passing this law, if such will be the case, wanted this freeze to continue until the Maritime Freight Rates Act is amended, it would have a political effect with which I would not want to be associated. Knowing how one's words can be twisted, I would fear that if I were associated with an amendment of that sort somebody might say about me: Why, that fellow Pickersgill had the nerve to suggest that parliament should amend the Maritimes Freight Rates Act, the charter of our liberties, the Magna Carta of the maritimes. I could not say in defence that I had not said it would be amended because in a bill of which I am the sponsor it would appear that the whole of parliament had said this act should be amended. If one were skilled enough at doing this sort of thing, which I am glad to say I am not, a lot of people might say that I intended to take that right away from them. I would advise the hon. member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings, who has only been elected once, not to jeopardize his chances of re-election by leaving himself open to that kind of misconstruction and imputation.

Therefore I do not think it would be a wise thing to do.
Although it would not make much difference legislatively, I do not think it would be a wise thing to do from the standpoint of a proper understanding in the Atlantic provinces of the intent of parliament. I think our intent is perfectly clear, that in freezing the rates in that area only as a temporary expedient, and associating that freeze with the facts which are known to everyone in the area, the problem is being dealt with urgently and there is a spur to get on with the job, whereas if the freeze was indefinite I fear that parliament would not have the same incentive. For that reason I really hope that the hon. gentleman will not press for the adoption of either of his suggested amendments.

So far as deferring to the minister's political assessment of the situation in the maritimes is concerned, with respect, Mr. Chairman, I must part company with him there. There is some concern in the maritimes now about the uncertainty of the freeze for two years. At the end of the two years rates are obviously going to go up. The

minister mentioned that there might be some new proposal on the basis of the Atlantic provinces transportation study, but that will be debated at another time. We are still going to have to debate the Maritime Freight Rates Act. If we could put something in the Maritime Freight Rates Act now, it might shorten that debate.
I fully appreciated the minister's remarks and for that reason I have restricted my remarks. This is the purpose I would hope to achieve. The people in the maritimes know that the freeze is going to end. The minister has said that the government is going to move. I find it difficult to reconcile the two views. How is the government going to be stimulated into action? The Maritime Freight Rates Act will continue but the new transportation commission will be able to adjust the rates and up the rates will go.
It was suggested by some witnesses before the transport committee that these rates would go up as much as 50 per cent. I appreciate the minister's remarks concerning the legislative imperfections in both amendments. I certainly defer to the minister's political assessment; I know the minister is only too capable of handling political affairs. While my experience in elections is relatively slight, I feel fairly certain where I stand on this point. I know the minister will be able to take care of himself in a like fashion. Therefore, unless the minister is prepared to consider some change in the proposed section and perhaps give an example of how the government will take the initiative two or three years hence, I am afraid I am going to have to move formally the amendment which I suggested last night.

Let me read his words again:
Subsection (1) shall be in force during the two years after the coming into force of subsection (1) and shall continue in force after the said two years unless, and until, the Maritime Freight Rates Act is amended to retain the historic intent and purpose of providing Atlantic provinces industry access to the markets of Canada without the handicap of distance.
I suggest, and I think the hon. member has agreed already, that all the words beginning with "to retain the historic intent and purpose" are meaningless. In other words, sir, the freeze would continue until amendments were made to the Maritime Freight Rates Act. These amendments might be ones which would bring no joy whatever to the hearts of shippers or the general population in the Atlantic provinces.
It seems to me that the motion the hon. member is making has a second very sharp edge. It is true that the provision of this amendment might bring about improvement of the Maritime Freight Rates Act. It is equally true, because susceptible of judgment based on opinion, that it might trigger an amendment that would work precisely the opposite way.
As evidence that this could be the case, I adduce the hon. member's own amendment. His amendment refers to retaining the historic intent and purpose of providing industry in the Atlantic provinces with access to the markets of Canada without the handicap of distance. I argue that the historic intent and purpose of the Maritime Freight Rates Act long since has been so badly eroded that the act which the hon. gentleman is now seeking to retain no longer performs the original intention of the enacting parliament. I am not at all zealous to see the act retained if it is not
improved in some way. I want to see an improvement. In other words, sir, I think that the purpose of the hon. gentleman is a good one. We all like to hedge in times of uncertainty. We like to put in a hedge that creates a presumption in our own favour.
But the amendment proposed here does not do that at all. In fact, it implies that the change could be a change against us. Any change in the terms of the Maritime Freight Rates Act could have the effect of thawing the freeze. We who come from the Atlantic provinces should recognize the actual situation. We should recognize that something is going to have to be done. But we do not now have the information upon which to base a scheme for the solution of our problem. Consequently, our best protection is to remain alert until the information is available. We must remain alert until we are ready to proceed to attempt the kind of solution to the problem of transportation in the Atlantic provinces that is desirable.

This legislation has been mooted for a long time. I am sure that in the past people have insisted that it should be brought in within a two-year period, but nothing like this has happened. speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, new section 336 deals with a number of aspects to which some members on this side of the house have already made numerous references during consideration of clause 1 of the bill, particularly before the Christmas recess. I participated in that debate and devoted considerable time to the precise subject under examination specifically in clause 33. My feelings today with regard to the provisions in this section are well known to the minister and to other members of the committee. I beg your indulgence, Mr. Chairman, if for the next few minutes my comments seem a repetition of previous ones. It is necessary to repeat certain things and to press the arguments advanced particularly by my province of Manitoba in concert with the other prairie provinces in relation to the main considerations of section 336.
The two specific subjects covered in section 336 are the maximum rate formula and the machinery and procedure for its application, and the process whereby a captive shipper may be identified under the terms of the legislation. The west has been particularly unhappy with the maximum rate formula as prescribed in the new legislation, as you know,
January 19, 1967

sir, and with the mechanics by which it will be applied. It is to that aspect of this section that I address myself for the next few moments this afternoon.
As has been said by other members of the house, including myself, without the costing data from the railways that the western provinces have repeatedly asked for it has been extremely difficult, in fact well nigh impossible, to assess the impact of the maximum rate formula correctly. The west was unhappy with section 329. The west is not unhappy with the way section 329 was amended. But the west is unhappy with much of section 336.
As I have said, in the past few years my province has been in the vanguard of the fight to develop in this country a comprehensive, efficient and progressive transportation policy and a national transportation approach. I think the minister will concede that point.
[DOT] (4:40 p.m.)
Some of the most reasoned and articulate arguments advanced with respect to transportation before this house and before the standing committee on transportation during the past five or six years were prepared by the province of Manitoba which worked in concert principally with the other western provinces. No one would disagree that Manitoba has played a signal role in the vanguard of the fight for a better transportation system and policy, and nowhere has its role been better demonstrated than in the major brief which it submitted to our standing committee last fall.
That brief was probably two to three years in preparation and represented some seven to eight years of application and study on the part of the Manitoba transportation people and members of the provincial administration at the research level. I think it would be presumptuous of me, and highly wasteful of the time of hon. members, if I were to try to express my own opinions and attitudes about this question to the exclusion of the specific formal arguments already advanced by my province. Therefore I beg the indulgence of the Chair and the committee to permit me to read into the record specific statements, recommendations and conclusions contained in the Manitoba brief. That brief contains so much expertise and so much sound and valid judgment that I do not think it should be pigeonholed at the standing committee level. I could not improve on it and therefore will refer to specific passages in it.
Transportation
Two transportation consultants from the United States were retained by the province of Manitoba in the course of preparation of the brief. They were university professors, Professor D. H. Borts and Professor Ernest W. Williams Jr. Their expertise and experience were heavily relied upon during the course of the deliberations in which the Manitoba transportation people engaged and a good deal of their research and conclusions were imbedded in the arguments advanced in the Manitoba case.
There was complete compatibility among these two professors, the experts from the provincial administration, and the legal counsel retained by Manitoba who contributed to the drafting of the brief, in regard to the contention that new section 336 contains a great many flaws and weaknesses and is inequitable in its treatment of the maximum rate formula, the application of that formula, and its provisions relating to a captive shipper and the identification of a captive shipper.
On this point I would like to refer to the Manitoba brief:
Two aspects of section 336 require attention. First, the applicability of the maximum rate formula which involves the definition of a captive shipper and the determinability of a captive shipper. Second, that dealing with the formula itself.
The royal commission in dealing with this problem recommended that all shippers should have the right to declare themselves captive. At page 104 (page 52) volume II, the commission stated:
"The decision to seek captive status must rest with the shipper. His reasons for initiating the action will be dissatisfaction with the rate he is forced to pay "
The legislation, as presented, envisages that even shippers who are now manifestly captive must establish this fact by special application to the commission. It is difficult to understand why the legislation requires that those intended to benefit from the royal commission recommendation be subjected to this difficulty of establishing their right to a maximum rate. It should be remembered that the royal commission designed the formula as an alternative to the present class rate structure. All shippers in Canada have the right to a class rate on the movement of their own commodities and this right does not entail an obligation to ship a given portion of their goods.
The commission at page 110 (page 55) stated:
"...Our problem, as we see it, is to attempt to substitute a more realistic method of maximum rate control for the traditional class rate maximum, which will protect the captive shipper and not limit the operation of commercial principles in the growing competitive sector."
The royal commission on a number of occasions referred to the Freight Rates Reduction Act. This act in itself was evidence of the parliament of Canada's determination that class and non-competitive commodity shippers were at least shippers to whom the term "captive" could apply because

January 19, 1967
Transportation
it was these shippers that the parliament of Canada determined should be relieved of the excessive burden caused by the last general freight rate increase in 1958. We are now advised in the provisions of Bill C-231 that the only captive shipper is one in respect of whose goods there is no alternative, effective and competitive service by a common carrier other than a rail carrier...
We are now faced with the situation where it is suggested that the only likely recipients of protection under the legislation are class rated shippers who represent 1 per cent of the tonnage carried by Canadian railways.
This was a point stressed in a telegram sent to the Prime Minister by the premier of Manitoba, the Hon. Duff Roblin, in concert with at least one and possibly both of the premiers of the other prairie provinces, at the time that the standing committee on transportation was considering the Manitoba brief last fall.
The brief continued:
In the 1965 waybill analysis the class rated traffic represented 1.7 per cent of the tonnage and approximately 4.6 per cent of the total revenues of the railways. If we are to accept this position we must assume that the intent of the legislation is to leave, without any control mechanisms, approximately 98 per cent of the traffic. In addition, members of the committee must remember that the existing class rates are, in fact, the maximum which the railways are permitted to charge any shipper in Canada.
These are rates granted to the shippers not by the gratuitous act of the railways, not by contract, but by the regulatory authority. If the above definition of captivity is to be accepted, there would be introduced a most alarming concept into rate-making in this country. We would have a situation where the present class rates are done away with, where all rules and regulations relative to unjust discrimination and unreasonableness of rates are eliminated, where a new maximum rate formula is introduced, the impact of which is unknown since cost data has been denied.
[DOT] (4:50 p.m.)
Both United States experts to whom I have referred made similar comments with regard to the maximum rate formula and the difficulty a captive shipper has. They made submissions to both the province of Manitoba and the standing committee on transportation. I believe it is important that some of their arguments be read into the record now. The submission made by Professor Borts had this to say on the subject, under the heading "definition of captivity":
Under the section 336 of the Bill C-231, a shipper of goods may request the commission to determine the probable range within which a fixed rate would fall should the shipper choose to apply for captivity. After being informed by the commission of the probable rate, the shipper may apply to the commission for captivity and the commission, after investigation, may fix a rate which is determined by the rate formula. The weakness of this provision

is that there is only a vague criterion specified by which the commission may decide whether a shipper is worthy of captive treatment. This vague definition is provided in the opening words of the section, where it is said that:
"a shipper of goods for which in respect to those goods there is no alternative, effective and competitive service by a common carrier other than a rail carrier or carriers or combination of rail carriers may, etc."
There is no specific pinpointing of the definition or criteria to be used in respect of a captive shipper under that terminology.
It is very difficult to specify what is meant by the absence of alternative, effective and competitive service. From one point of view, there is very little competitive service in Canada, where there are only two railway systems to begin with, and where truck lines are also owned by these very same railway systems. While there may be a wide range of services which are technologically effective they may not be economically competitive. On the other hand, we know that the rails have lost traffic to the trucks so we know there are shippers with alternatives. The difficulty is how to define the absence of such alternatives. This opening section 336	(1) is faulty in not indicating what
constitutes the absence of alternative service.... The traffic which is truly captive in the economic sense consists of heavy loading commodities which find the railroads more advantageous than truck because of the present technology and cost of rail and truck operations. This represents such a broad category of traffic, however, that it is probably best not to tie up the time of a commission staff in deciding who is and who isn't economically captive. The best way to define captivity is through self-declaration by the shipper. Any shipper should be free to ask the commission to specify a rate which he would enjoy if he should declare himself captive.
Then the submission continues:
In determining the rate to be charged captive shippers, the commission is instructed to fix a rate equal to the variable cost of the carriage of the goods and an amount equal to 150 per cent of the variable cost.
I submit that this is a thoroughly charitable arrangement under which the railways are permitted to operate. It would be a fairly generous arrangement if any business or entrepreneur were in the position of being paid 150 per cent over and above his variable costs in a given competitive commercial situation. No satisfactory answer has been given to members of the standing committee or members of this house concerning the procedure that was followed in arriving at the figure of 150 per cent. No one has pinpointed the source of that figure, nor has anyone explained why it should be 150 per cent. Nevertheless, that happens to be the rate which now, presumably, is to be embedded in this legislation for all time to come.
Mr. Borts in his submission points out that the legislation sets out a very complicated cost
January 19, 1967

formula, the effect of which is to provide a mark-up of 150 per cent over variable cost for shipments of 30,000 pounds. For shipments of larger than 30,000 pounds the peculiar provisions of this formula pile mark-up upon mark-up, because the economies of heavy loading traffic are not reflected in the artificial variable cost concept to be calculated. In an earlier submission to the Department of Transport by eight provinces, an analysis of the cost formula revealed that the mark-up over variable cost varied from 150 per cent of variable cost on a 30,000-pound load to a mark-up of 600 per cent of variable cost for a shipment of 140,000 pounds. The percentage mark-up over variable cost rose continually as carload weight rose because of the failure of the rate formula to take account of the economies of heavier loads.
This, Mr. Chairman, is the nub or focal point of the whole argument of the west in respect of this section, that is, that the provisions of the maxium rate formula as presently envisaged by this legislation militate against economy and efficiency in a normal business sense from the point of view of both the railways and the shipper. No account is taken of the possible economies or benefits which might accrue from the heavier loadings. In fact a mockery is made of the heavier loadings and the economies possible from such practice. The maximum rate formula as proposed in this legislation destroys any incentive for rail efficiency in this regard.
At this point I should like to refer to a specific argument which is incorporated in the Manitoba brief. I should like to quote this directly in order to emphasize the point:
-the proposed formula in Bill C-231 would create a most inequitable situation. The formula includes a fixed percentage (150 per cent) above variable cost, which percentage is related to no known factor. If the costs of the railways increase by $1 the shipper's maximum rate will increase by $2.50 (150 per cent). It similarly would destroy any real incentive for improving rail efficiency since for each reduction in unit cost of $1 the railway would be subject to a $2.50 loss in revenue. This was not the decision of a commission directed to determine inequities in the railway freight rate structure- to relieve the burdens on captive shippers and to recommend policies for achieving more efficient operation of the transportation system of Canada.
There is extensive and intensive evidence and weight of argument contained in the submission by the province of Manitoba to which I have referred to buttress the argument I am attempting to advance on this occasion to the effect that section 336 with its provisions respecting the maximum rate formula and the captive shipper will militate against the best
Transportation
interests of the competitive economic system and the benefits which should accrue from that type of system to the shippers and the railroads of western Canada as a whole as well as to the economy of western Canada in general.
[DOT] (5:00 p.m.)
On the same subject the following is what Professor Ernest W. Williams had to say:
The concept of a formula based upon a 30,000 pound carload-
This is the basis for the maximum rate formula in the legislation.
-advanced by the royal commission is at variance with that commission's apparent objective to afford a measure of protection against the undue imposition of overhead burdens upon shippers where they lack an effective economic alternative to rail transport. It appears to me, also, as undesirable to incorporate in a statute a fixed percentage to be applied over variable costs. The relationship between variable and total cost in a railroad system is likely to change over time and it ought not to be necessary to amend a statute in order to recognize such a change. The origin of the 150 per cent is not adequately explained in the report of the royal commission but the mark-up over variable cost required by the railways ought to be related to their revenue requirements which will change over time. Bill C-231 is silent on this point.
Later Professor Williams submits:
Shippers have traditionally been entitled to just and reasonable rates from common carriers without regard to the presence or absence of competition.
The following is also stated later in his submission:
The proposition that competitive reductions in rail rates designed to meet competitive forces outside the control of the railways may be tied to an undertaking by shippers to forward traffic by rail is sound and is one of the important advantages of the Canadian agreed charge system. But it is far from equally clear that a shipper should be required to commit himself to the movement of his traffic by rail as a condition for securing a reasonable maximum rate in the place of one which exceeds the standard.
When I spoke on this and related subjects on December 21 I made the point that the maximum rate formula and its application were a source of considerable concern to a number of us on the standing committee because it seemed to us that under this particular clause of the proposed legislation the railways were being given carte blanche to charge whatever the traffic would bear in western Canada. It certainly seems to me and to those who worked on the preparation of the Manitoba brief that this is a situation and attitude which are hardly conducive to a healthy economy in western Canada.

January 19, 1987
Transportation
I have a chart here from which I should like to quote to illustrate some of the tremendous advantages of mark-ups and profits which accrue to the railway company where heavier car load shipments are involved. The legislation as it is presently worded provides that the maximum rate imposed on a captive shipper shall consist of the variable cost plus 150 per cent on 30,000-pound carload lots. As the lots increase in size the variable costs really go down from the point of view of percentage. The maximum rate a shipper must pay also goes down fractionally, but the mark-up over the variable cost and the profit to the railway go up by astronomical amounts.
As the Manitoba brief pointed out, the maximum rate formula in Bill C-231 does not give the shipper the benefit accruing from the reduction in unit cost because of heavier loading. The committee might be interested in some of the percentages and specific mathematics which illustrate that point. Based on 150 per cent of variable costs on 30,000 pounds the proposed formula results in a 6.6 per cent reduction in rate on 50,000 pounds, 9.9 per cent on 70,000 pounds, 11.5 per cent on 90,000 pounds and 12.6 per cent on 110,000 pounds. These data are taken from the Interstate Commerce Commission figures for the United States, based on a 500-mile haul.
Under the maximum rate formula provided by Bill C-231 the maximum rate for 30,000 pounds is 1.82 cents per 100 pounds and the maximum rate for 120,000 pounds is 1.59 cents for 100 pounds. The rail revenue per car is, therefore, $546 for a 30,000-pound movement and $1,908 for a 120,000-pound movement. What should be particularly noted is that a shipper of a 30,000-pound carload is required to contribute only $328.20 per car toward the railway overhead whereas the shipper of a 120,000-pound carload is compelled to contribute $1,615.20 per car.
The production of a more equitable maximum rate formula requires that one or more of the assumptions on which Bill C-231 is founded must be changed. That is suggested by the Manitoba brief and is an argument to which I entirely subscribe. The brief states that it is necessary and that the formula requires revision both to reflect the economics of the heavier loading and the percentage relationship of the contribution to total variable costs.
As further illustration of that particular point I should like to refer to a chart which I have in front of me, prepared by Professor Borts. It is an assessment of the development

of maximum rates and mark-ups over actual variable cost in Bill C-231 and is based on Canadian Pacific Railway costs in 1953, as derived from the royal commission report, on a 500-mile haul. It gives the following breakdown. On a 30,000-pound carload lot the variable cost, which includes the cost of money, is 50.2 cents; the mark-up over the actual variable cost in that case is 150 per cent. When the carload lot goes up to 50,000 pounds the variable cost goes down to 34.1 cents. The mark-up over the actual variable cost goes up to 246 per cent. At 70,000-pound carload lots the variable cost is reduced to 27.2 cents. One of the natural laws in business is that there is an economy to be derived from heavier loading, but the mark-up over actual variable cost and the profit to the railway goes up.
This chart pursues this argument through various levels of carload lots and finally demonstrates that a carload lot of 130,000 pounds has a variable cost of 19.4 cents-

I thank the minister and members of the committee for their kindness in permitting me to continue. I really am coming to a conclusion and I will take only two or three more minutes of the committee's time.
I was making the point that in respect of a 130,000-pound carload lot the variable cost comes down to 19.4 cents. This is a reduction in the variable cost from that for a 30,000-pound load of 30.8 cents. The variable cost has been constant through all these figures at $1.26. The maximum rate is based on the 150 per cent formula. The mark-up over the actual variable cost and profit to the railway is 467 per cent.
The conclusion one must inevitably draw from these figures is that it is not worth the railway companies' time and, therefore, not in their best interests to strive for efficiency in rail loadings.
January 19, 1967

[DOT] (5:10 p.m.)
If their variable cost is reduced, under the formula as it is presently constituted and composed their mark-up, their margin of profit is reduced by a far more substantial amount. The degree and speed with which the mark-up rises would reflect itself in the reverse; the mark-up would be reduced in equally dramatic fashion if the railway were to reduce its costs and bring the figure for variable costs down to a more reasonable level and practice these rail efficiencies which are vital to the improvement of the transportation system of this county. Therefore we argue that the formula as it is designed militates against those economies and prevents the shippers and the railways themselves taking advantage of the economies of heavier loadings. There are not economies of heavier loadings in the section as now written.
Finally, Mr. Chairman, I wish to return to the subject of the captive shipper and the definition of "captive shipper". It is a subject to which I referred in my initial remarks in this debate on December 21. The experts who prepared the Manitoba presentation and argument felt that the wording in new section 336 <1) is entirely unsatisfactory on the subject of the captive shipper and the definition of "captive shipper". They felt that it does not in fact properly define a captive shipper at all, and takes away and denies much of the protection that was supposed to be embedded in this legislation for various shippers in the country as a result of the studies undertaken by the MacPherson royal commission, which as we know really led to the developement of this legislation.
I would therefore propose, in line with the proposal that has already been made by the administration of Manitoba through its brief presented to the standing committee, that a new subsection be written into new section 336. I am not at this juncture proposing it as a formal amendment, but I suggest that while debate on this section continues it might be advantageous if hon. members on both sides of the house would give some thought to a subsection that would more clearly define a captive shipper. I request the continued good will of the minister in this respect and ask him to ponder the suggestion during the next few minutes while debate on this section continues. The amendment I suggest is that a new subsection be added as subsection (2) of section 336 as follows:
A shipper of goods in respect of which the rates in effect on the 1st day of January, 1965, were class and commodity rates subject to the Freight
Transportation
Rates Reduction Act, shall be deemed to have no alternative, effective and competitive service by a common carrier other than a rail carrier or carriers or combination of rail carriers.

Mr. Chairman, I was keenly interested in the remarks of the hon. member for Winnipeg South because I was wondering whether he had courage enough to try to alter new section 336 so it would serve some useful purpose in this bill. I have looked at this section very carefully and considered many ways and means of trying to improve it. I have considered moving amendments to the section which would provide some effective maximum rate control where it is needed. I am sorry to advise the commmittee that I do not believe the section can be repaired. Therefore I propose to move later that it be deleted from the bill. I say this knowing full well that there are shippers in Canada who are completely dependent on railway freight services for the operation of their business.
I suggest that there is no effective maximum rate control provided in section 336. I have reached this conclusion in view of the discussions we have had a number of times on this question. Fictitious loading factors are used, such as 30,000 pounds, and there is an allowance of 150 per cent above the unknown variable costs that goes into this formula. Therefore it seems to me we would be better off without it.
On December 20 I dealt with this matter very carefully and outlined what I thought to be the weaknesses in section 336. I gave those reasons to the house when the bill was first returned from the standing committee on transport and communications. I do not intend to repeat all those arguments because the minister and the members of that standing committee know that during the course of the debate in the committee I attempted to obtain certain cost date that I regarded as essential in order to calculate what would be the effect of the passage of this bill. I failed to convince the members of that committee that it was essential and that we had the power to send for it. I am sorry that happened but nevertheless that is the case.
Having considered this clause and compared it with clause 16, which has been dealt with during the course of this debate and was considered by the standing committee, I am convinced that if section 336 in clause 53 were deleted the entire reliance for maximum rate control would be placed in clause 16. In my opinion that would be far, far better than trying to make a shipper who thinks he may be captive prove captivity under the definition

January 19, 1967
Transportation
in this clause and, even if he did, to have this formula applied.
I believe this section is useless. If it were deleted the shippers of Canada would rely entirely on clause 16 if they wanted to appeal against a rate being demanded of or imposed on them. I think it would be well to draw the attention of hon. members of this committee to the wording of clause 16 so they will understand what I am arguing. I hope they will agree with me; I also hope the minister will agree with me. If it is proven that the public interest if affected there is, of course, authority under clause 16 given to the new transportation commission, first, to investigate the matter and then, under subclause (4) of clause 16, it has the power to make an order to remedy the situation. I would far, far rather rely on the wording in that clause than I would on the wording in section 336. Clause 16 (2) provides:
Where a person has reason to believe-
(b) that the effect of any rate established by a carrier or carriers pursuant to this act or the Railway Act after the commencement of this act, may prejudicially affect the public interest in respect of tolls for or conditions of the carriage of traffic-
And so on. In that event the shipper may make application to the transportation commission for leave to appeal the rate. If the commission is satisfied that a prima facie case has been made it is obliged to make an investigation of this matter. After that investigation is made the provisions of subclause (4) will apply. Subclause (4) reads as follows:
[DOT] (5:20 p.m.)
If the commission, after a hearing, finds that the act, omission or rate in respect of which the appeal is made is prejudicial to the public interest, the commission may, notwithstanding the fixing of any rate pursuant to section 336 of the Railway Act but having regard to section 334 of that act, make an order requiring the carrier to remove the prejudicial feature in the relevant tolls-
We argued long and hard with the minister to have something of this nature included in the act, and now it is here. However, what I fear is that if the provisions of section 336 are left in the act and a shipper feels he is paying an unreasonably high rate, a rate which may be discriminatory or, in other words, a rate higher than that paid by another shipper on the same commodity and under similar conditions, the commission may refer him to section 336 in which a remedy may be found. But there is no effective remedy to be found in it. As far as we can determine the maximum rate in applying the formula and the factors included in section 336 would be of absolutely

no benefit. We are unable to make any calculations because we have not been provided with data on the so-called variable costs so that we cannot establish what the rate might be on certain commodities in relation to the present rate.
As I said over and over again in the committee, I think that members of this house not only have the right but have the responsibility to ascertain what the effect of the legislation is likely to be. In other words, we should have sufficient information to enable us to anticipate what will be the various fluctuations in the rates, or at least some samples of the rates if the new law that we are being asked to pass is in fact applied. We cannot do that without all the factors used in the formula and the variable costs which were requested. There were some samples respecting sulphur, lumber, steel, dressed beef and so on, and I moved a motion in this regard. We were not asking for specific rates that were being charged by the railways to any specific shipper but we wanted to have samples so that we could use the 30,000-pound base, with changes in the loads to 50,000 pounds and 70,000 pounds, and add the 150 per cent provided under section 336 to see what the end result of these calculations would be. We cannot do this because we do not have the variable costs which are so essential in these calculations.
One other important reason in support of my argument is that the president of the C.P.R. and the chairman of the board of the C.P.R., as well as the minister himself, said before the standing committee that they could not think of anyone who would qualify as a captive shipper. The only point which the minister would concede was that someone who paid class rates might be considered a captive shipper. The minister knows very well that less than 5 per cent of the freight being moved at present is charged at class rates. He knows also that some of the other class rates in effect today are as much as five or six times the normal rate that is in effect. I can think of a few examples such as coal. I talked to the coal operators who were down here in Ottawa and they told me what the hon. member for Kootenay East has said. May I say that the Canadian Pacific Railway has no competition; it is a monopoly. It is in facing that fact that we will find the answer to many of the difficulties of the coal shippers. Let me go one step further and tell you that when arrangements were made for coal to be sent to Japan, port facilities were set up to load and unload the coal and our thought was that these facilities would not only be used for the loading of coal but also for loading potash shipped from Saskatchewan, and a lot of other bulk products which would spread the cost over the various types of commodities and therefore reduce the cost of loading coal. We were quite willing to agree to a certain rate on bulk loading and we were quite willing to assume that when the volume increased the cost of loading should drop. We had statistics on the cost of moving this coal from the ports on the West coast to Japan. However, now that the Japanese are using their own ships, the rates on the hauling of coal have declined, but the saving is unknown.
The miners said they would not strike and agreed to the $16 or $18 a day which they were getting at that time. We thought that if a chip could be taken off the cost of loading at Vancouver, a chip taken off the profits of the operators when the volume was increased, and a chip taken here and there all along the line, together it would amount to the government subsidy.
The hon. member for Kootenay East said that a difference of $2.73 cannot be made up. Let me remind him that in the beginning it was $4.50. When the former government set the exchange rate on the dollar, that reduced the subsidy substantially. I think that if the government took the bull by the horns and really tried to get rid of the $2.73, they could do so. Let the hon. member for Kootenay East mark my words when I say that in less than a year's time the C.P.R. will be setting rates on

captive shippers, who in turn will be asking the commission to fix rates which will be much higher than the $5.30 which is being paid today. I think the hon. member for Kootenay East will agree with me that we are striving to increase our import trade.
Slightly under a billion tons of coal are being shipped to Japan, and a lot of thought, labour and effort has gone into arranging these shipments. We want to expand this trade. If the hon. member for Kootenay East were as successful in getting a commuter train so as to reduce the costs, and get the C.P.R. to put into effect more modern methods, then the people in the Crowsnest pass would be in clover. The only way in which he thinks it can be done is by threatening to establish a railway which would be hooked up to the Northern Pacific. For those who are not familiar with the situation let me explain that box cars are loaded with coal in the Crowsnest pass and then wait a few days until a train comes along. They are then hooked on to the train, which may take a week of bumping along before it arrives at its destination at a port on the west coast. The cost of moving coal in that way is very high.
Is the C.P.R. going to modernize and change this obsolete method of moving coal or do they intend to ask the commission to accept the rates and costs as they exist today? These are the problems that I see in the bill. These are the obstacles to doing what I think should be done, namely to facilitate our export trade. I do not feel that competition in transportation-certainly in the west and on the Atlantic coast-is sufficient to warrant the conditions that we have set up in the bill, and here I am referring to section 336 in particular.

This afternoon the hon. member for Winnipeg South set forth very pertinent and concise information which I think gives conclusive proof that section 336 is not satisfactory to a great portion of this country.
The views of Manitoba, and those of Professors Borts and Williams, are very well set forth indeed. I must say that I agree with those gentlemen in their consideration of this particular problem. The difficulty with which they were faced was a matter of costing figures. They pointed out that it was impossible to get accurate cost figures because the committee and these gentlemen were unable to get up-to-date costing figures from the Canadian Pacific. The only figures that they could use were those the MacPherson commission had obtained. They then tried to bring those figures up to date as well as they could. They were able to get information from the United States on cost figures, and they tried to relate this information to the situation in Canada. This is one of the reasons we felt that the bill is ineffectual, and that proposed section 336 in particular will not do what it is intended to do.
In particular, I object to this section because it uses the basis of a carload of 30,000 pounds. Having sat in the committee for weeks on end, I know the explanation for the use of this 30,000 pounds. It was used, we were told, because it is a suitable truckload. In my opinion this is a fallacious argument because a railway is not going to use a 30,000-pound load just because the trucking people find it efficient to operate on that basis. I believe therefore the whole of the proposed
Transportation
section 336 is rendered ineffective because that 30,000 pound weight is established as the standard carload weight.
As I said a moment ago, the hon. member for Winnipeg South has pointed out the effect of this on loads of a greater weight, and it could be as much as 400 per cent. The hon. member was only using loads of up to 130,000 pounds, so what the effect would be on the potash shipper who now uses something like 200,000-pound cars beggars description. It certainly would allow the railroads, if they were using this as a basis on which to cost their potash shipments, to charge astronomical rates. I know that they do not do that because they negotiate with the potash shipper, who gets an agreed charge. The trouble there is that there is in effect only one thing that controls the cost to the potash shipper, and that is the law of charging all that the traffic can bear. I do not believe that that is good for the country. I do not believe this is a logical law to apply.
It could be argued that it is better for the railways to make large profits than for the potash shipper in our country, most of whom are financed by United States capital. Some people would argue it is better for the railways to make the profits than for United States capital to make money. I disagree, because if we are going to develop this country we must not have the profits going to the transportation means; they must go to those who are risking their money to develop the country. I am not one of those who feel it is wise for us to restrict the flow of capital to this country by allowing the railways to have the bulk of the profits as a result of charging all the traffic will bear. I would much prefer those profits to go to the potash mine, the iron mine, the copper developer and to the man who is boring the wildcat well. It is far better to have these people get the profits, so they will continue development.

Mr. Chairman, I had probably made the main points in my argument, but there are a couple of subsidiary ones I should like to emphasize and to which I want to direct the attention of the committee.
As I said before, I feel it unnecessary to repeat the arguments that the hon. member for Winnipeg South so ably presented. It has never been my feeling that as a member of parliament I should just parrot ideas that have already been expressed. Unless I have something new to say, then I do not feel it is necessary for me to say anything at all. However, I believe that there could be a little time spent looking at this proposed section 336, particularly at subsection (2) in which 150 per cent of the variable cost figure is set as a fixed rate applicable to the carriage of goods.
I think it ought to be understood by everyone that this figure of 150 per cent is a pragmatic one arrived at in actual fact by the MacPherson commission. The commission merely took a large number of cases, considered what they thought would be the normal cost factor, and then added to this 150 per cent of the variable cost, feeling that this would set a rather fair rate on which to evaluate total costs. But as I say, it is a pragmatic figure and consequently is open to the usual complaint which may be levelled against such figures. That is to say, it is a judgment figure and depends on the people who make the judgment. Therefore there is no reason why we should arrive at the same judgment.
While I hesitate to set any figure, I do think that we should very much qualify this figure in our minds in view of the fact that it is pragmatic and today, some years after the recommendations made by the MacPherson commission, could well be a figure that is not suitable at all.

That tolls shall always be charged equally to all persons if circumstances and conditions are substantially similar;
This was what was written into the old section 317 of the Railway Act. In other words, if two companies are manufacturing similar commodities and those commodities are hauled equal distances, then the rates would have to be the same. There could be no discrimination. The second point is:
That there be no discriminatory increase or reduction in tolls in favour of or against any user;
In other words, if you are going to give one company an agreed charge you must give the other company the same rate or that agreed charge is out. The third point is:
That tolls must not unjustly discriminate between different localities;
In other words, if you have a manufacturing company in southern Ontario and one in northern Ontario whose products are hauled over the same railroad for the same distance, those rates shall be the same. There shall not be a preferred rate for one company in one locality and a discriminatory rate for the other. The fourth point is:
That, unless the board is satisfied, no toll must be higher for a shorter than for a longer distance.

Alternative means "an interchange, alternating with another, succeeding each other by turns, consisting of alternating things." Effective is the key word in this phrase. We know that the key word in the Restrictive Trade Practices Commission legislation is "unduly," and under that legislation proof must be given that something is affecting the economy of the country unduly. In this phrase the key word is "effective," and its definition is, "having an effect, powerful in effect," and so on. One may have an alternative, but if that alternative has no effect then it does not have much use. The amendment sets out to remedy this deficiency, and states:
A shipper of goods in respect of which the rates in effect on the 1st day of January, 1965, were class and commodity rates subject to the Freight Rates Reduction Act, shall be deemed to have no alternative, effective and competitive service by a common carrier other than a rail carrier or carriers or combination of rail carriers.
The Freight Rates Reduction Act which came into effect in 1959 placed a freeze on freight rate increases on class and non-competitive rates. Anyone benefiting from that legislation could logically be expected to receive some protection in this clause of the amending bill, and should be accepted as a captive shipper. This is the whole essence of the argument.
The minister may declare that he is not particularly concerned about these things and that very few people will qualify as captive shippers. He can lecture us a great deal on the essence of competition, but I do not think
Transportation
anyone in Canada will say that the railways are 100 per cent public utilities. Surely the government must accept the fact that the railways have a duty to perform in those areas in which they have a monopoly, in which there is no effective alternative service. Shippers in those areas should be able to receive some protection under this clause.
A very noted transportation economist hired by the Manitoba government, Mr. Morrow, dealt at great length with the history of the Canadian transportation system. Our early governments aided the establishment of a railway system in order that it might provide a public service. I do not want to go into the history at length, but it is a fact that back in the early 1900's a public service was established. We set up the Board of Transport Commissioners to regulate and rule in respect of the public service provided by the railways. [DOT] (9:50 p.m.)
We have seen competition grow. We have seen Canada grow. There no longer is the same need for some of the protection which was given. No longer do we accept the fact that the railways are 100 per cent public utilities. Also we will not accept the fact that the railways are absolutely free corporate entities, because there still are areas in which they operate within a monopoly. In this area they still must be declared to be public utilities. There is a regulatory board which has some control over the Bell Telephone Company. Every other similar company generally is ruled by a public utilities board. The National Energy Board regulates the pipe line companies, because we give the pipe line companies a monopoly in respect of their operations within a given area. At one time these monopolies were in effect across Canada. Now we accept the fact that they are not monopolies in respect of the whole of Canada, but are monopolies in some areas.
The people who are producing goods, providing for the welfare of their families and contributing to the economy of Canada should be able to look to the government for protection, because the railroads were built with the intention that they would provide a public service. The railways accepted this obligation. This amendment says in effect that if there were non-competitive areas in 1959 there now may be non-competitive areas today, that these areas should be accepted as captive areas, and that they should come under the definition which relates to a captive shipper. It is all very well for the minister to tell us

Transportation
that they do not have to prove they are captive shippers, that they merely have to assert it.
