maintopic: TRANSPORT-DORION, QUE.-INQUIRY AS TO REPORT ON LEVEL CROSSING ACCIDENT
TRANSPORT-DORION, QUE.-INQUIRY AS TO REPORT ON LEVEL CROSSING ACCIDENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am deeply grateful to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pickersgill), for his kindness in accepting to remain in the house a little while longer, to consider a matter with which he is very familiar, but to which I would again like to draw his attention, since this is a very urgent question and one of deep concern, from the standpoint of public safety.
Every day we are faced with an increasing number of highway tragedies. In addition to these, we have accidents occurring at grade crossings and, among others, we note the tragedy which occurred at St. Clair, in Dorchester county. Not too long ago, two similar calamities occurred within a few days: one at Montmagny and another at St-Francois-de-Bellechasse. The people are getting more and more alarmed.
That is why, Mr. Speaker, I am renewing my efforts and asking the minister if something even more specific could be done, so as to eliminate what I would call deadly road hazards.
January 19, 1967	COMMONS
If that is not possible, I would like to suggest, in the first place, that we should seek additional' funds. In 1954, we had $5 million in the Railway Grade Crossing Fund. If I remember right, this amount was increased to $15 million in 1958, which represents quite a short lapse of time. Why? Because it was realized that traffic was increasing at a frightening rate and additional funds were required to satisfy the newly created needs of ever-increasing traffic.
We are now in the year 1967 and nothing has been added to the Railway Grade Crossing Fund since 1958. In order to even begin solving the problem, our Railway Grade Crossing Fund desperately needs replenishing.
I feel it is imperative that the Railway Grade Crossing Fund should be increased: $15 million is no longer enough.
Second, Mr. Speaker, I should like to refer to an editorial by Mr. Maurice Cham-poux, correspondent for La Presse. Mr. Cham-poux is an excellent newspaperman and I always enjoy reading his articles, because he has a very rich vocabulary and exceptional writing ability. However, upon reading his comments about one of my recent statements,
I noted that he had not quite grasped the full meaning of my observations. I said, amongst other things, that the municipalities cannot afford to apply for safety devices for their grade crossings because, as everyone knows, and above all the minister, the fund contributes 80 per cent of the cost in the case of a new safety device, the railway, 7J per cent, and the municipality or the local authority to which the road belongs, 12J per cent.
Many municipalities do not have the means to do so. I discussed the matter, not long ago, with the former president of the Union of Municipalities, the member for Riviere-du-Loup-Temiscouata (Mr. Gendron), who is well known as an authority on the matter. He confirmed the fact by saying that, out of the 1,700 municipalities in the province of Quebec, at least 1,200 are poor. The municipalities cannot afford to make the application.
Consequently, the act should be amended in this regard.
Third, Mr. Speaker, the procedure is too long before grade crossings can be obtained. In fact, the report of the Board of Transport Commissioners for the year ending December 31, 1965 says:
During 1965, the board received 2,584 applications under the various legal provisions related to the jurisdiction of the said board.
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion
The Board of Transport Commissioners lacks the time to deal with such problems, because it is too slow in answering these applications. I am asking the minister whether there is a way to change this jurisdiction and, when grade crossings are being sought, to make it possible to seek them from somebody other than the Board of Transport Commissioners which is unable to reply rapidly to applications in accordance with safety requirements.
This procedure should be changed, as I said, Mr. Speaker, to expedite matters. How do we proceed now? Municipalities make an application and the Board of Transport Commissioners consult with the railway company concerned. An inspection is made. Time is lost. Efforts are made to find money, and when it is found that no money is left, the application is finally held in abeyance. That is why many cases could have been settled if the procedure had been amended or changed to expedite things. I am appealing to the minister to improve the situation and I understand that he is sincere and well disposed toward me, because he knows that we must fight unmercifully against-I repeat-those deadly road hazards.

I think everyone realizes how desirable and important it is to eliminate really dangerous level crossings and to protect other level crossings. I do not think we adequately appreciate yet how much has been accomplished in this country in the last 15 years. The progress has been absolutely extraordinary. I was given some figures today that astonished me, though I probably ought to have known them; but one does not keep all these figures in one's head all the time.
As of September last year-these are the latest figures available-Ontario had 8,603 railway-highway crossings, and Quebec had 3,598. In Ontario 12.2 per cent of the crossings were grade separated, that is to say they were not level crossings at all, and in Quebec the figure was 12.3 per cent. In Ontario 22.9 per cent of the level crossings were protected; in Quebec, 30.5 per cent. If you add the two

January 19, 1967
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion together you find that the percentage in Ontario that we protected either by grade separation or other protection was 35.1 per cent; in Quebec, 42.8 per cent. This means it is getting very close to half for those in Quebec that are already protected. In Canada as a whole, unfortunately, the record is not so good. The only province better than Quebec in this regard is Nova Scotia; that happens to be the best province in the whole country.
[DOT] (10:10 p.m.)
I do not believe this parliament would hesitate to vote any funds needed in order to eliminate these hazards. NATURAL, GAS-TRANS-CANADA PIPE LINES- SUGGESTED TWINNING OF LINE IN CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the matter that I raised yesterday is not a new one to be raised in the house, but it throws some new information on the matter I had occasion to raise before. I am referring to the proposal of Trans-Canada Pipe Lines to build a trans Canada pipe line through the United States, a proposal which unfortunately has received the blessing of this government. My objections, the objections of my party and of many other Canadians to this proposal are no secret. We are opposed to it for three major reasons: first, because it will starve and blight the north country; second, because it will place the necks of the Canadian customers in the noose, in that the decisions, rules and regulations concerning a resource as vital as natural gas and upon which Canadian industry will depend will be subject to rules, regulations and decisions made in a foreign country, and we do not think this is any favour to Canadian customers. Our third objection is to the fact that we will be accepting a very-bad precedent-pipe lines being the transportation of the future-and setting a very bad

example by building our transcontinental pipe lines through a foreign country.
I was very surprised this week to hear officials of the ministers' department claim that there is no objection, particularly in the north country, to this proposal of the government. I have here partial returns of a questionnaire which we sent out across the country to see what the people felt about this proposal. I can make it available to the minister and to any of his officials, if they wish to have it. I would like to list a few of these returns. From the riding of Cochrane, out of 377 returns only two were in favour. In Timmins out of 488 there was only one in favour. In Fort William out of 456, three were in favour. In Port Arthur out of 674, two were in favour. In Kenora Rainy River, out of 366, one was in favour. In Algoma East-the riding of the Prime Minister-out of 205 replies, three were in support of the government stand. In Algoma West, out of 355 replies, 15 were in favour. I discovered that this was due to the fact that they had been misinformed to the extent that they were told that the only hope of getting Canadian gas was through the American line, and yet for the last five years Canadian gas was only 80 miles away, at Blind River. In Sudbury and Nickel Belt, out of 542 replies there were three favouring the government stand, and while the returns are not compiled completely from Timiskaming and Nipissing, out of approximately 1,000 replies, four favoured the government. This means that out of 4,500 replies less than three-quarters of 1 per cent backed the government stand on this particular proposal.
I think it would be of benefit to the minister and to hon. members if I put on the record an excerpt from a letter which was sent to the Sault Star on December 7 dealing with this proposal. It is somewhat of a fantasy, but it shows what would have happened if the same kind of thinking that goes on today had been in effect 100 years ago. This is the story:
It is the year 1878 and Prime Minister Sir John A. Macdonald has just announced that instead of building the proposed Canadian Pacific Railway over the frozen wasteland and rocks of Canada as originally proposed, it would be built through the United States at a great saving. The railway will now be called the Atchison, Topeka and the C.P.R.
It is the year 1937 and Prime Minister Mackenzie King has announced that a coast to coast airline has been founded. Terminals will be built in the United States at a great saving on heating costs. He stated that it was a wonderful achievement for a country with a population of a hundred thousand people. The new airline will be known as the Minnesota, Michigan and Air Canada Ltd. Passengers may transfer from Detroit by dog team to the unspoiled, uninhabited area known as Sault Ste. Marie.
January 19, 1967

News Bulletin. Dateline has stated that since Canada has refused to accede to his demand that they (Canada) cease sending wheat to Lower Slobovia, action will immediately be taken.
President Silverwater reaches for a button in his office which controls the pump for the Trans-Canada Pipe Lines...
Maybe this is somewhat fantastic but this is exactly what would have happened 100 years ago if the thinking of the present government had been adopted at that time. However, Mr. Speaker, it would appear we are going to be saved by the bell from our own foolishness. If we look at the Globe and Mail of yesterday we find it reports that the holding of additional hearings will result in postponement of the final decision by the United States Federal Power Commission until late this year. Then the article says that when the commission finally disposes of the issue, first taken up more than two years ago, there is a possibility any ruling it would make would be challenged in the United States courts, causing still further long delays.
This means of course that we can confidently expect to wait two years before any decision is made. Trans-Canada has committed itself to this government to the effect that by 1970, three years from now, they are prepared to start looping the northern line. We say that they should start this now. We say that this government should urge and insist that they start it now. There is no denying the fact that this government has made out a case, and the energy board has given proof, of the desperate need that is growing in southern Ontario and Quebec for gas. It is well known that the north is short of it now. You can ask any industry from Kenora, to Dryden, to Kapus-kasing or Sudbury, and they will all say they are short of gas.
The energy board has been telling Trans-Canada for the last three years that they should increase the gas supply. There is no excuse for any postponement. There is no excuse for waiting another two years, only to be turned down by the United States power commission and then try to repair the damage. This article in yesterday's Globe and Mail asserts again what we have been saying before the energy board, that Trans-Canada officials have said they would never join Northern Gas in any gas exchange scheme, insisting that they would enlarge their line in Canada rather than accept this alternative.
I should like to impress upon the minister that the responsibility toward Canadian customers in the north and south is not the responsibility of Trans-Canada. Their
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion responsibility is only to their own company and their own shareholders. It is only the government of Canada that has responsibility to the Canadian people and responsibility for our resources. Let us accept that responsibility. Let us start now. Let this government tell Trans-Canada to get on with the job. If they are short of money, we will lend them money. We did it before, and they paid it back.

I am sure that if the hon. member had been asked about the value of the questionnaire sent out by the hon. member for Lapointe to his constituents, asking whether or not he should remain in the house as a separatist, he would have said it was not worth the paper on which it was written.

The last part is a historical review, while the first part describes the attack made by Northern Natural Gas Company, a United States company on the Great Lakes project. I am sure the hon. member is the first one who would want us to respect the law.

POLLUTION-REQUEST FOR FURTHER RESEARCH INTO DETERGENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, one of the first conditions which drew the attention of the public to water pollution was the appearance of foam or suds on the surface of the water. While this was not the most dangerous type, it was the most noticeable. Much of it was caused by detergents used in the home for washing, and in industry in the manufacture of textiles, paints and other products.
In Canada a campaign was put on by the manufacturers of detergents to reduce the sudsing effect. A completely new ingredient known as LAS, or linear alkylate sulfonate, was substituted for the sudsing component. This new chemical is bio-degradable; in other words, it decomposes in sewage plants to a degree of about 95 per cent and eliminates foaming to all intents and purposes. The Canadian Manufacturers of Chemical Specialties have confirmed that the Canadian manufacturers of detergents have now completely converted to this new product. A word of commendation is due to them for their effort in this regard, effected at considerable
DEBATES	January 19, 1967
expense. The appearance of Canadian waters should noticeably improve in 1967.
My question to the minister related to the continuation of research in this field. Although the appearance of waters may improve, the nutrient component is still there. Detergents have not been made pure, because they will still provide the nutrients which induce algae growth. In a way the situation may be more dangerous because public fears may subside when the foaming is no longer visible. Furthermore, there are other sources of water pollution than detergents. I am asking for confirmation from the minister that research in this very important area will be pressed forward even more strongly in 1967.

speakeroldname: Hon. Jean-Luc Pepin (Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources):
speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
maintopic: POLLUTION-REQUEST FOR FURTHER RESEARCH INTO DETERGENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am quite willing to agree with my hon. friend on the progress that industry has made in this field, but I am very eager to agree with him that the changeover to non-frothing detergent soaps by the manufacturers merely corrects the ugly formation of foam in the receiving waters. This change has, unfortunately, as the hon. member said, no effect on the phosphate content of detergents or on the removal of this constituent in waste water treatment. The government, through the co-operation of several departments and the International Joint Commission, is continuing to conduct research on the phosphate problem through the programs of investigations on the great lakes. The hon. member is aware of that. He is also aware that I consider the research presently done by the federal government on the great lakes, where the federal government has clear jurisdiction, a symbol of the government's willingness to contribute to the solution of the pollution problem. In the coming years the great lakes will be our great federal laboratory-if you put it this way-the laboratory in which we shall find the answer to pollution problems.
Requests for research grants totalling about $40,000 to universities and research institutes relating to phosphates are currently being considered by one government department. I can assure my hon. friend that we shall do our best. I am grateful, as usual, for his constant prompting.
